name: MK-0773
lead: MK-0773, also known as PF-05314882, is an experimental steroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) that was developed to increase muscle mass and strength while minimizing effects on other tissues. It was tested in clinical trials for sarcopenia, the age-related loss of muscle mass and function [1][2][11].

The appearance appeal follows a chain: a compound that activates the androgen receptor in muscle would raise lean mass, which in turn would give a fuller, more muscular physique, while its tissue selectivity was designed to spare the prostate, skin oil glands and reproductive tissues that conventional androgens affect [3][11]. Its discovery was reported in 2010 as the product of a screening strategy using more than 1,000 synthetic androgen receptor ligands to look for compounds whose anabolic and reproductive-tissue effects were separable [3].

In a phase 2A trial in 170 frail older women with sarcopenia, it increased lean body mass compared with placebo, but this did not translate into improved strength or physical function [1]. Wikipedia reports that development was abandoned after the Merck and GTx collaboration ended in early 2010, and the compound is not approved for any use [11].

paras: MK-0773 is a 4-azasteroid with the formula C27H34FN5O2 and a molar mass of about 479.6 g/mol, and Wikipedia describes it as a more advanced version of the related compound TFM-4AS-1 [11]. A doping-control paper notes that, unlike most SARMs, which are nonsteroidal, MK-0773 has a 4-aza-steroidal nucleus and undergoes considerable metabolic transformation [9].

MK-0773 is an androgen receptor ligand chosen using the idea that anabolic effects in muscle and effects in reproductive tissue depend on different transcriptional requirements, so a partial agonist might separate them.[3]

According to Wikipedia, it acts as a potent partial agonist of the androgen receptor (reported efficacy of about 78 percent in transactivation assays), does not bind the progesterone or glucocorticoid receptors, cannot be converted to estrogen by aromatase and barely inhibits 5-alpha-reductase [11]. In animal studies its maximal lean-mass effect was reported as about 80 percent of that of dihydrotestosterone (DHT), with much smaller effects on the uterus, seminal vesicles and sebaceous glands [11]. Like DHT it lowered total and HDL cholesterol in the cited human work [11].

The one published efficacy trial found lean mass gains without functional benefit (see Clinical studies).[1] A 2025 systematic review of randomized trials of SARMs on physical performance covers this class of compounds more broadly.[4]

A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2A trial (NCT00529659, started 2007) enrolled 170 women aged 65 or older with sarcopenia and moderate physical dysfunction. Participants received MK-0773 or placebo for six months, and all received vitamin D and protein supplementation.[1][5] MK-0773 produced a statistically significant increase in lean body mass versus placebo, but the authors concluded this did not translate into better strength or function, and noted that improvements in the placebo group may be partly attributable to the supplements.[1]

Two phase 1 trials are also registered as completed: one in healthy postmenopausal women (67 participants, listed under osteoporosis, begun 2005) and one in healthy older men (68 participants, begun 2007). Their results have not been published.[6][7] A review of SARMs for cancer-related muscle wasting also discusses the compound class.[8] Wikipedia reports that in human studies the compound produced anabolic effects with little or no effect on sebaceous glands, endometrium or prostate, and that elevated liver enzymes were associated with it in trials [11]. A 2025 systematic review of nine SARM studies in 970 patients covered six SARMs including MK-0773 and evaluated physical performance, body composition and safety [4].

Merck and GTx developed MK-0773, with clinical trials in sarcopenia beginning in late 2007; the collaboration ended in early 2010 and GTx stopped development soon after [11]. The compound's discovery strategy, published in 2010, used a large set of androgen receptor ligands to show that anabolic and reproductive-tissue effects can have different transcriptional requirements [3]. SARMs were added to the World Anti-Doping Agency's Prohibited List in 2008, and none had received full clinical approval by 2018 [8].

Doping-control researchers have identified in vitro phase I metabolites of MK-0773 to support detection, and SARMs are covered by anti-doping surveillance.[9][10] No established use of MK-0773 in looksmaxxing communities is documented. A review of SARM misuse notes that easy internet access leads some amateurs to use SARMs despite the health risks [10]. Wikipedia notes that MK-0773 has also appeared as a novel designer drug [11].

card.summary: Steroidal SARM that added lean mass in frail older women but did not improve strength or function in a phase 2 trial.
card.note: Investigational only; lean mass gain did not translate to function in the one efficacy trial.

quick.overview:
MK-0773 is an investigational SARM that was tested for sarcopenia, the loss of muscle with age. It was designed to act on muscle with less effect on other tissues.
In the one published efficacy trial, 170 older women gained lean mass compared with placebo, but strength and physical function did not improve beyond placebo.
quick.mechanism: It is a steroidal androgen receptor ligand picked from a large screen of compounds for partial, tissue-selective activity.
quick.risks: It is not approved for any use and is covered by anti-doping testing.

chain: Oral steroidal SARM binds the androgen receptor
Muscle tissue responds with anabolic signalling
Lean body mass rises while reproductive-tissue effects stay low
angle.text: MK-0773 was designed to build lean mass through a tissue-selective androgen receptor effect. In the one published efficacy trial, lean mass rose versus placebo in older women, while strength and function did not improve beyond placebo.
